claim: The eukaryotic phylum Apicomplexa encompasses thousands of obligate intracellular parasites of humans and animals with immense socio-economic and health impacts.
source: The eukaryotic phylum Apicomplexa encompasses thousands of obligate intracellular parasites of humans and animals with immense socio-economic and health impacts.
evidence: This is a general statement about Apicomplexa that draws from established scientific knowledge about this phylum.

claim: Chromera velia and Vitrella brassicaformis are free-living non-parasitic photosynthetic algae closely related to apicomplexans.
source: We sequenced nuclear genomes of Chromera velia and Vitrella brassicaformis, free-living non-parasitic photosynthetic algae closely related to apicomplexans.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript and references to previous work.

claim: Proteins from key metabolic pathways and from the endomembrane trafficking systems associated with a free-living lifestyle have been progressively and non-randomly lost during adaptation to parasitism.
source: Proteins from key metabolic pathways and from the endomembrane trafficking systems associated with a free-living lifestyle have been progressively and non-randomly lost during adaptation to parasitism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative genomic analysis presented in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: The free-living ancestor contained a broad repertoire of genes many of which were repurposed for parasitic processes, such as extracellular proteins, components of a motility apparatus, and DNA- and RNA-binding protein families.
source: The free-living ancestor contained a broad repertoire of genes many of which were repurposed for parasitic processes, such as extracellular proteins, components of a motility apparatus, and DNA- and RNA-binding protein families.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary analysis of gene gains and losses, and the identification of orthologs between chromerids and apicomplexans.

claim: Based on transcriptome analyses across 36 environmental conditions, Chromera orthologs of apicomplexan invasion-related motility genes were co-regulated with genes encoding the flagellar apparatus.
source: Based on transcriptome analyses across 36 environmental conditions, Chromera orthologs of apicomplexan invasion-related motility genes were co-regulated with genes encoding the flagellar apparatus, supporting the functional contribution of flagella to the evolution of invasion machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data and co-expression analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: More than 5000 apicomplexan species have been described to date.
source: More than 5000 species have been described to date, and over 1 million apicomplexan species are estimated to exist (Adl et al., 2007; Pawlowski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Over 1 million apicomplexan species are estimated to exist.
source: More than 5000 species have been described to date, and over 1 million apicomplexan species are estimated to exist (Adl et al., 2007; Pawlowski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Apicomplexans possess an abundance of specific classes of nucleic acid-binding proteins with regulatory functions in parasitic processes.
source: Despite their diverse host tropism (Roos, 2005) and life cycle strategies, apicomplexans possess several unifying molecular and cellular features, including the abundance of specific classes of nucleic acid-binding proteins with regulatory functions in parasitic processes (Campbell et al., 2010; Flueck et al., 2010; Radke et al., 2013; Kafsack et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Apicomplexans possess extracellular proteins for interactions with the host.
source: Despite their diverse host tropism (Roos, 2005) and life cycle strategies, apicomplexans possess several unifying molecular and cellular features, including the abundance of specific classes of nucleic acid-binding proteins with regulatory functions in parasitic processes (Campbell et al., 2010; Flueck et al., 2010; Radke et al., 2013; Kafsack et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014), extracellular proteins for interactions with the host (Templeton et al., 2004a; Anantharaman et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Apicomplexans possess an apical complex comprising a system of cytoskeletal elements and secretory organelles.
source: Despite their diverse host tropism (Roos, 2005) and life cycle strategies, apicomplexans possess several unifying molecular and cellular features, including the abundance of specific classes of nucleic acid-binding proteins with regulatory functions in parasitic processes (Campbell et al., 2010; Flueck et al., 2010; Radke et al., 2013; Kafsack et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014), extracellular proteins for interactions with the host (Templeton et al., 2004a; Anantharaman et al., 2007), an apical complex comprising a system of cytoskeletal elements and secretory organelles (Hu et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Apicomplexans possess an inner membrane complex (IMC) derived from the alveoli.
source: Despite their diverse host tropism (Roos, 2005) and life cycle strategies, apicomplexans possess several unifying molecular and cellular features, including the abundance of specific classes of nucleic acid-binding proteins with regulatory functions in parasitic processes (Campbell et al., 2010; Flueck et al., 2010; Radke et al., 2013; Kafsack et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014), extracellular proteins for interactions with the host (Templeton et al., 2004a; Anantharaman et al., 2007), an apical complex comprising a system of cytoskeletal elements and secretory organelles (Hu et al., 2006), an inner membrane complex (IMC) derived from the alveoli (Eisen et al., 2006; Kono et al., 2012; Shoguchi et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Apicomplexans possess a non-photosynthetic secondary plastid, termed the apicoplast.
source: Despite their diverse host tropism (Roos, 2005) and life cycle strategies, apicomplexans possess several unifying molecular and cellular features, including the abundance of specific classes of nucleic acid-binding proteins with regulatory functions in parasitic processes (Campbell et al., 2010; Flueck et al., 2010; Radke et al., 2013; Kafsack et al., 2014; Sinha et al., 2014), extracellular proteins for interactions with the host (Templeton et al., 2004a; Anantharaman et al., 2007), an apical complex comprising a system of cytoskeletal elements and secretory organelles (Hu et al., 2006), an inner membrane complex (IMC) derived from the alveoli (Eisen et al., 2006; Kono et al., 2012; Shoguchi et al., 2013), and a non-photosynthetic secondary plastid, termed the apicoplast (McFadden et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Chromerids comprise single-celled photosynthetic colpodellids closely associated (and likely symbiotic) with corals.
source: Chromerids comprise single-celled photosynthetic colpodellids closely associated (and likely symbiotic) with corals (Cumbo et al., 2013; Janouškovec et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis demonstrates that chromerid algae are closely related to Apicomplexa.
source: Phylogenetic analysis demonstrates that these algae are closely related to Apicomplexa (Janouškovec et al., 2013), confirming the long-standing hypothesis that apicomplexan parasites originated from a free-living, photosynthetic alga (McFadden et al., 1996; Moore et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the phylogenetic analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The phylogenetic relationship between chromerids and Apicomplexa confirms the long-standing hypothesis that apicomplexan parasites originated from a free-living, photosynthetic alga.
source: Phylogenetic analysis demonstrates that these algae are closely related to Apicomplexa (Janouškovec et al., 2013), confirming the long-standing hypothesis that apicomplexan parasites originated from a free-living, photosynthetic alga (McFadden et al., 1996; Moore et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the phylogenetic analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The Chromera velia nuclear genome was assembled into 5953 scaffolds totaling 193.6 million base-pairs.
source: A shotgun approach was used to sequence and assemble the Chromera and Vitrella nuclear genome into 5953 and 1064 scaffolds totaling 193.6 and 72.7 million base-pairs (Mb).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the sequencing and assembly data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Vitrella brassicaformis nuclear genome was assembled into 1064 scaffolds totaling 72.7 million base-pairs.
source: A shotgun approach was used to sequence and assemble the Chromera and Vitrella nuclear genome into 5953 and 1064 scaffolds totaling 193.6 and 72.7 million base-pairs (Mb).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the sequencing and assembly data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The disparity in genome size between Chromera and Vitrella is attributable largely to the presence of transposable elements totaling ∼30 Mb in Chromera vs only 1.5 Mb in Vitrella.
source: The disparity in genome size is attributable largely to the presence of transposable elements (TEs) totaling ∼30 Mb in Chromera vs only 1.5 Mb in Vitrella, as the predicted number of protein-coding genes is almost the same at 26,112 and 22,817, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genome assembly and annotation data.

claim: Chromera has 26,112 predicted protein-coding genes.
source: The disparity in genome size is attributable largely to the presence of transposable elements (TEs) totaling ∼30 Mb in Chromera vs only 1.5 Mb in Vitrella, as the predicted number of protein-coding genes is almost the same at 26,112 and 22,817, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the gene prediction data.

claim: Vitrella has 22,817 predicted protein-coding genes.
source: The disparity in genome size is attributable largely to the presence of transposable elements (TEs) totaling ∼30 Mb in Chromera vs only 1.5 Mb in Vitrella, as the predicted number of protein-coding genes is almost the same at 26,112 and 22,817, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the gene prediction data.

claim: On the phylogenetic tree, Chromera and Vitrella formed a group closest to the apicomplexan clade.
source: On the phylogenetic tree (Figure 1A), Chromera and Vitrella formed a group closest to the apicomplexan clade, consistent with previous phylogenies (Moore et al., 2008; Janouškovec et al., 2010, 2013, 2015; Oborník et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: The long branches from the common node of Chromera and Vitrella are consistent with drastic differences in morphology, life cycle, plastid and mitochondrial genomes between the two chromerids.
source: The long branches from their common node are consistent with drastic differences in morphology, life cycle (Oborník et al., 2012), plastid (Janouškovec et al., 2010) and mitochondrial genomes (Flegontov et al., 2015) between the two chromerids (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic tree in Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Divergence of the proto-apicomplexan ancestor from the alveolate ancestor (Stage I) was accompanied by losses of 1668 and gains of 2197 orthogroups.
source: Divergence of the proto-apicomplexan ancestor from the alveolate ancestor (Stage I) was accompanied by losses of 1668 and gains of 2197 orthogroups (sum of the two 'pies' in Stage I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transition of the free-living proto-apicomplexan ancestor to the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) is accompanied by many gene losses (3862 orthogroups) but few gains (81 orthogroups).
source: Transition of the free-living proto-apicomplexan ancestor to the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) is accompanied by many gene losses (3862 orthogroups) but few gains (81 orthogroups) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Divergence of coccidians from the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage III) is characterized by modest changes (537 losses; 414 gains).
source: Divergence of coccidians, for example, Toxoplasma gondii, from the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage III) is characterized by modest changes (537 losses; 414 gains), whereas divergence of hematozoans, for example, Plasmodium spp., is marked by drastic losses (1384 losses; 77 gains) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Divergence of hematozoans from the apicomplexan ancestor is marked by drastic losses (1384 losses; 77 gains).
source: Divergence of coccidians, for example, Toxoplasma gondii, from the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage III) is characterized by modest changes (537 losses; 414 gains), whereas divergence of hematozoans, for example, Plasmodium spp., is marked by drastic losses (1384 losses; 77 gains) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Paucity of gained genes (81 orthogroups) during Stage II indicates that the genome of the free-living ancestor possessed most of the genes that were present in the common ancestor of apicomplexans and survived in their present-day descendants.
source: Paucity of gained genes (81 orthogroups) during Stage II indicates that the genome of the free-living ancestor possessed most of the genes that were present in the common ancestor of apicomplexans and survived in their present-day descendants.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the gene gain/loss analysis.

claim: The inferred proto-apicomplexan ancestor, like present-day chromerids, possessed complete metabolic pathways for sugar metabolism, assimilation of nitrate and sulfite, and photosynthesis-related functions.
source: The inferred proto-apicomplexan ancestor, like present-day chromerids, possessed complete metabolic pathways for sugar metabolism, assimilation of nitrate and sulfite, and photosynthesis-related functions (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Appendix 2, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B and supplementary materials.

claim: Both Chromera and Vitrella initiate heme synthesis in the mitochondrion using aminolevulinate synthase (C4 pathway).
source: Unlike in other photosynthetic algae, both Chromera and Vitrella initiate heme synthesis in the mitochondrion using aminolevulinate synthase (C4 pathway), which thus far has been found only in a few eukaryotic heterotrophs, such as Euglena gracilis, dinoflagellates, and apicomplexans (Kořený et al., 2011; van Dooren et al., 2012; Danne et al., 2013) (Appendix 2 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Both chromerids and apicomplexans encode modular multi-domain fatty acid synthase I (FASI)/polyketide synthase enzymes and single-domain FASII components.
source: Both chromerids and apicomplexans encode modular multi-domain fatty acid synthase I (FASI)/polyketide synthase enzymes and single-domain FASII components (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Treatment of Chromera with a FASII inhibitor triclosan showed decreased production of long chain fatty acids.
source: Treatment of Chromera with a FASII inhibitor triclosan showed decreased production of long chain fatty acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Appendix 2), suggesting that Chromera synthesizes short-chain saturated fatty acids using the FASI pathway, which are then elongated using the FASII pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Chromera synthesizes short-chain saturated fatty acids using the FASI pathway, which are then elongated using the FASII pathway.
source: Treatment of Chromera with a FASII inhibitor triclosan showed decreased production of long chain fatty acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Appendix 2), suggesting that Chromera synthesizes short-chain saturated fatty acids using the FASI pathway, which are then elongated using the FASII pathway.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the triclosan treatment experiment.

claim: Transition to an apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) was accompanied by the loss of metabolic processes including photosynthesis and sterol biosynthesis.
source: Transition to an apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) was accompanied by the loss of metabolic processes including photosynthesis and sterol biosynthesis (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The apicomplexan ancestor appeared to possess a significant complement of enzymes in various pathways.
source: The apicomplexan ancestor appeared to possess a significant complement of enzymes in various pathways (Figure 2B) (Lim and McFadden, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by the metabolic pathway analysis shown in Figure 2B and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The proto-apicomplexan had a nearly complete repertoire of the endomembrane trafficking complexes.
source: The proto-apicomplexan had a nearly complete repertoire of the endomembrane trafficking complexes, and much of this repertoire persisted through to the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II) (Hager et al., 1999; Klinger et al., 2013a) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Appendix 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the endomembrane trafficking analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, and citations to previous studies.

claim: All known components of flagella were present in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor.
source: All known components of flagella were present in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: Most of the flagellar components were retained in the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II), but losses occurred as apicomplexan lineages differentiated (Stage III).
source: Most of the components were retained in the apicomplexan ancestor (Stage II), but losses occurred as apicomplexan lineages differentiated (Stage III).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: Components of intraflagellar transport were lost in all apicomplexan lineages except in coccidians.
source: Components of intraflagellar transport, which are typically essential for assembling flagella, were lost in the other lineages except in coccidians (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: The basal body proteins were lost from piroplasms.
source: The basal body proteins, which support an organizing center for microtubules, were lost from piroplasms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis.

claim: Some striated fiber assemblin (SFA) proteins were maintained in all apicomplexan lineages including piroplasms.
source: Some striated fiber assemblin (SFA) proteins, typically associated with basal body rootlets, were maintained in all apicomplexan lineages including piroplasms (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B,D); their presence has been hailed as evidence that some flagellar-proteins are repurposed for new functions in apicomplexans (see below) (Francia et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B,D and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Genes encoding extracellular proteins exported into the host environments were over-represented among those gained after Stage III.
source: Genes encoding extracellular proteins exported into the host environments were over-represented among those gained after Stage III (Figure 3), suggesting that adaptation to specific hosts was accompanied by expansion of extracellular proteins mediating host–parasite interactions (Templeton et al., 2004a; Anantharaman et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Stage III was accompanied by gains of genes encoding DBD proteins, mostly apiAP2 proteins.
source: Stage III was accompanied by gains of those encoding DBD proteins, mostly apiAP2 proteins (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting extensive regulatory changes mediated by apiAP2 proteins during lineage differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Stage II was accompanied by over-represented gains of various cytoskeletal components, including alveolins, those of the actomyosin complex and glideosome-associated proteins.
source: Stage II was accompanied by over-represented gains of various cytoskeletal components, including alveolins, those of the actomyosin complex (e.g., myosins) and glideosome-associated proteins with multiple membrane spans 1 and 3 (GAPM1 and GAPM3), suggesting that the molecular machinery powering gliding motility, which is essential for host cell invasion arose during evolution to apicomplexans (Frenal et al., 2010) (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Appendix 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Gene gains during Stage I were over-represented by proteins with 'RBD abundant in Apicomplexans' (RAP).
source: Gene gains during Stage I were over-represented by proteins with 'RBD abundant in Apicomplexans' (RAP, Pfam: PF08373) (Lee and Hong, 2004), many of which were conserved as one-to-one orthologs across descending lineages, suggesting development of evolutionarily conserved functions before apicomplexans and chromerids diverged (Figure 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the evolutionary age analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins.
source: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins (Appendix 4), including GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility (Bullen et al., 2009), and the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans (Poulin et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromerid genomes encode GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility.
source: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins (Appendix 4), including GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility (Bullen et al., 2009), and the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans (Poulin et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Chromerid genomes encode the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans.
source: Chromerid genomes encode many orthologs of apicomplexan cytoskeletal proteins (Appendix 4), including GAPM2, a member of an important protein family for apicomplexan cytoskeletal structure and gliding motility (Bullen et al., 2009), and the IMC sub-compartment protein family (ISP), implicated in establishing apical polarity and coordinating the unique cell cycle of apicomplexans (Poulin et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Chromerid genomes encode numerous apiAP2 proteins, more abundant than dinoflagellates.
source: Importantly, chromerid genomes encode numerous apiAP2 proteins, more abundant than dinoflagellates, suggesting that they have expanded in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor after it split from dinoflagellates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Many of the chromerid apiAP2 proteins belong to putative paralogous clusters, suggesting that their expansion was driven by gene duplication.
source: Many of the chromerid apiAP2 proteins belong to putative paralogous clusters, suggesting that their expansion was driven by gene duplication (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Appendix 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and is an inference based on the data.

claim: Only a small subset of the apiAP2 proteins are shared across apicomplexans.
source: Only a small subset of the apiAP2 proteins are shared across apicomplexans, suggesting that the large apiAP2 complement in the proto-apicomplexan ancestor has diversified independently in descending lineages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and is an inference based on the data.

claim: For 11 out of 12 orthogroups with RAP domains, co-expressed orthogroups overlapped significantly between P. falciparum and Chromera.
source: For 11 out of 12 orthogroups with RAP domains, co-expressed orthogroups overlapped significantly (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.05) between P. falciparum and Chromera, suggesting involvement of RAP proteins in cellular processes evolutionarily conserved across apicomplexans and chromerids (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RAP and their co-expressed orthogroups encode proteins with putative mitochondrial import signals more often than expected by chance in Chromera and P. falciparum.
source: RAP and their co-expressed orthogroups encode proteins with putative mitochondrial import signals more often than expected by chance in Chromera and P. falciparum (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.05) (Figure 4B), and also in other apicomplexans and chromerids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the subcellular localization prediction analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Three Toxoplasma RAP genes with predicted mitochondrial localization signals are localized to the mitochondrion.
source: We have randomly chosen three Toxoplasma RAP genes with predicted mitochondrial localization signals (Supplementary file 6) and confirmed experimentally by 3′ endogenous gene-tagging with reporter epitopes that all three are localized to the organelle (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental localization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Cryptosporidium lineage that has a highly reduced mitochondrion lacking both the genome and most canonical metabolic pathways is the only apicomplexan group to have also lost its RAP repertoire.
source: Consistent with this, the Cryptosporidium lineage that has a highly reduced mitochondrion lacking both the genome and most canonical metabolic pathways (Abrahamsen et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2004) is the only apicomplexan group to have also lost its RAP repertoire (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and citations to previous studies.

claim: The frequency of co-expression amongst 80 orthogroups comprising genes functionally annotated as implicated in invasion processes in the free-living Chromera was significantly higher than expected by chance.
source: Among the 1918 orthogroups, we identified 80 orthogroups comprising genes functionally annotated as implicated in invasion processes. The frequency of co-expression amongst them in the free-living Chromera was significantly higher than expected by chance (p < 0.0005), suggesting pre-existing functional relationships before transitioning to parasites (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In one of the co-expression modules, 9 out of 10 orthogroups are co-expressed with a gene encoding SFA (Cvel_872).
source: In one of the co-expression modules (numbered 1 in Figures 4E), 9 out of 10 orthogroups are co-expressed with a gene encoding SFA (Cvel_872), a key protein for organizing the basal bodies of the flagellar apparatus in algae and the apical complexes in apicomplexans (Kawase et al., 2007; Francia et al., 2012) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4E and 4F, and citations to previous studies.

claim: SFAs are the only flagellar components found in all apicomplexans tested.
source: We note that SFAs are the only flagellar components found in all apicomplexans tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the flagellar component analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: For 9 out of 10 orthogroups in the co-expression module with SFA, their co-expressed orthogroups in Chromera overlapped significantly with those in P. falciparum.
source: Also in this module, for 9 out of 10 orthogroups, their co-expressed orthogroups in Chromera overlapped significantly with those in P. falciparum (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.05), indicating that their regulatory programs have been evolutionarily conserved (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The co-expression module with SFA includes various types of genes implicated in host cell invasion processes of apicomplexans such as genes encoding rhoptry protein ROP9, apical sushi protein ASP, and gliding motility components GAP40 and GAPM2.
source: This module include various types of genes implicated in host cell invasion processes of apicomplexans such as genes encoding rhoptry protein ROP9, apical sushi protein ASP, and gliding motility components GAP40 and GAPM2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-expression analysis and functional annotation of genes in the module.

claim: The apical complex has been postulated to have emerged from the flagellar apparatus and associated cellular transport systems in free-living algae, based on ultrastructural evidence.
source: The apical complex has been postulated to have emerged from the flagellar apparatus and associated cellular transport systems in free-living algae, based on ultrastructural evidence (Okamoto and Keeling, 2014; Portman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the free-living ancestor, some of the genes implicated in the invasion process of present-day apicomplexans were functionally associated with those implicated in flagellar motility.
source: These results suggest that, in the free-living ancestor, some of the genes implicated in the invasion process of present-day apicomplexans were functionally associated with those implicated in flagellar motility, providing the much-needed genetic evidence for the postulate.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the co-expression analysis.

claim: A group of functionally related proteins associated with the flagellar apparatus was repurposed as a module of the apical complex and became a foundation for the invasion machinery.
source: We speculate that a group of functionally related proteins associated with the flagellar apparatus was repurposed as a module of the apical complex and became a foundation for the invasion machinery.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the co-expression analysis and evolutionary inference.

claim: The transition to parasitism was accompanied by massive genomic loss that continued as its descendants became specialized intracellular parasites infecting diverse hosts.
source: Analysis of Chromera and Vitrella genomes has enabled insights into how apicomplexan parasites have evolved from free-living ancestors. The transition to parasitism was accompanied by massive genomic loss that continued as its descendants became specialized intracellular parasites infecting diverse hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene gain/loss analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The genome of free-living photosynthetic ancestors encodes many component proteins previously assumed to be restricted to the parasitic apicomplexan lineages.
source: The genome of free-living photosynthetic ancestors encodes many component proteins previously assumed to be restricted to the parasitic apicomplexan lineages.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative genomic analysis showing orthologs of apicomplexan proteins in chromerids.

claim: Pre-existing components in the free-living ancestor, including those of what would later become part of the invasion machinery, were co-opted during evolution to facilitate a successful parasitic lifestyle in multiple hosts.
source: Such pre-existing components, including those of what would later become part of the invasion machinery, were co-opted during evolution to facilitate a successful parasitic lifestyle in multiple hosts.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparative genomic and co-expression analyses.

claim: The genome of the proto-apicomplexan ancestor served as a molecular blueprint for evolution of the most successful group of eukaryotic parasites known to date.
source: The genome of the proto-apicomplexan ancestor served as a molecular blueprint for evolution of the most successful group of eukaryotic parasites known to date.
evidence: This is a concluding statement that summarizes the main findings and is an inference based on the entire study.
